mediterranean-cuisine.name: Mediterranean triad
mediterranean-cuisine.summary: The idea, popularised by cookery writer Elizabeth David's 1950 book, that Mediterranean cooking centres on three core elements: olive, wheat and grape, yielding oil, bread and pasta, and wine.

emmer.name: Emmer wheat
emmer.summary: A hybrid wheat species domesticated in the Near East, one of the first crops grown there; widely farmed in the ancient world, it survives today mainly in mountain regions.

cleruchy.name: Cleruchy
cleruchy.summary: A specialized type of colony that Athens established in Classical Greece, its name meaning "lot-holder"; the practice was later adopted by Hellenistic kingdoms too.

solon.name: Solon
solon.summary: Athenian statesman, lawmaker and poet (c. 630–560 BCE), one of the Seven Sages of Greece, credited with reforms that laid the foundations of Athenian democracy.

pythagoras.name: Pythagoras
pythagoras.summary: Ancient Greek philosopher and polymath (c. 570–495 BC) from Samos, founder of Pythagoreanism, later credited with the Pythagorean theorem and the doctrine of transmigration of souls.

pliny-the-elder.name: Pliny the Elder
pliny-the-elder.summary: A Roman author, naturalist and military commander (23/24–79 AD) who wrote the 37-volume encyclopedia Natural History and died attempting to rescue people during the eruption of Vesuvius.

plato.name: Plato
plato.summary: An ancient Greek philosopher (c. 428–347 BC) considered the foundational thinker of Western philosophy, who founded the Academy in Athens and developed the Theory of Forms.

winged-victory-of-samothrace.name: Winged Victory of Samothrace
winged-victory-of-samothrace.summary: Hellenistic Greek marble statue of the goddess Nike, dating to about 190 BC, now displayed at the top of the main staircase in the Louvre in Paris.

venus-de-milo.name: Venus de Milo
venus-de-milo.summary: An ancient Greek marble statue of Aphrodite, dated to around 160–110 BC, found on Milos in 1820 and displayed in the Louvre since 1821 as one of the most famous ancient sculptures.

milos.name: Milos
milos.summary: A volcanic Greek island in the Cyclades, source of famous sculptures including the Venus de Milo, with a population of about 5,193 as of 2021.

dying-gaul.name: Dying Gaul
dying-gaul.summary: An ancient Roman marble statue of a wounded Celtic warrior, copied from a lost Greek Hellenistic bronze possibly commissioned around 230–220 BC by Attalus I of Pergamon to mark his victory over the Galatians.

laoco-n-and-his-sons.name: Laocoön and His Sons
laoco-n-and-his-sons.summary: An ancient marble sculpture depicting the Trojan priest Laocoön and his sons attacked by sea serpents, excavated in Rome in 1506 and long displayed in the Vatican Museums.

dorians.name: Dorians
dorians.summary: One of the four major ancient Greek ethnic groups, including Sparta and Corinth, distinguished by their dialect; rivalry with the Ionians contributed to the Peloponnesian War.

mycenae.name: Mycenae
mycenae.summary: An archaeological site in Greece that was a major military stronghold and centre of Greek civilization in the second millennium BC, giving its name to the Mycenaean period.

helen-of-troy.name: Helen of Troy
helen-of-troy.summary: A figure in Greek mythology considered the most beautiful woman in the world, whose marriage to Paris of Troy was said to have caused the Trojan War.

skene-theatre.name: Skene
skene-theatre.summary: The structure at the back of an ancient Greek stage, originally a tent, that evolved into the elaborate backdrop from which the word 'scene' derives.

red-figure-pottery.name: Athenian red-figure pottery
red-figure-pottery.summary: A style of ancient Greek pottery developed in Athens around 520 BCE, with figures left in the natural red or orange colour of the clay against a painted black background.

alexander-the-great.name: Alexander the Great
alexander-the-great.summary: King of Macedon from 336 BC who conquered much of the known world by age 30, creating an empire stretching from Greece to India; tutored by Aristotle.

odeon-building.name: Odeon
odeon-building.summary: An ancient Greek and Roman building used for musical performances, singing and poetry competitions, generally smaller than a theatre and roofed for better acoustics.

ai-khanoum.name: Ai-Khanoum
ai-khanoum.summary: Ruins of a Hellenistic Greek city in northern Afghanistan, founded around 300–285 BCE under the Seleucid dynasty, that later served the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom until its destruction around 145 BCE.

leonidas-i.name: Leonidas I
leonidas-i.summary: King of Sparta (c. 540–480 BC) of the Agiad dynasty who led the allied Greek stand at Thermopylae in 480 BC against the Persian invasion, dying there and becoming a legendary hero of the '300 Spartans'.

thermopylae.name: Thermopylae
thermopylae.summary: A narrow pass in Greece, site of the Battle of Thermopylae between Greek and Persian forces, and named for its hot sulphur springs.

xerxes-i.name: Xerxes I
xerxes-i.summary: Persian king (c. 518-465 BC) who ruled the Achaemenid Empire from 486 BC, famed for his 480 BC invasion of Greece that won early victories but ended in defeat at Salamis and Plataea.

battle-of-salamis.name: Battle of Salamis
battle-of-salamis.summary: A naval battle in 480 BC in which an outnumbered Greek fleet under Themistocles defeated King Xerxes' Achaemenid Persian fleet near Athens, marking a turning point in the Persian invasion of Greece.

themistocles.name: Themistocles
themistocles.summary: Athenian politician and general (c. 524–459 BC) who built up the Athenian navy and helped secure the decisive Greek victory over Persia at the Battle of Salamis in 480 BC.

salamis-island.name: Salamis
salamis-island.summary: The largest Greek island in the Saronic Gulf, close to Athens' port of Piraeus, whose main port Paloukia connects it to the Athens urban area by ferry.

hoplite.name: Hoplite phalanx
hoplite.summary: The tightly packed formation of armored Ancient Greek citizen-soldiers armed with spears and shields, adopted from the 8th century BC and dominant in Greek warfare.

achaean-league.name: Achaean League
achaean-league.summary: A confederation of Greek city-states in the Peloponnese, most notably from 280 BC, defeated by Rome in 146 BC in an event that ended Greek independence.

battle-of-corinth-146-bc.name: Battle of Corinth
battle-of-corinth-146-bc.summary: A 146 BC battle in which Rome crushed the Greek city-state of Corinth and its Achaean League allies, ending Greek independence; Corinth was afterward burned and its people killed or enslaved.

achaean-war.name: Achaean War
achaean-war.summary: The 146 BC war in which Rome defeated the Achaean League, ending mainland Greece's independence and marking the start of direct Roman control there.

aspis.name: Aspis
aspis.summary: A heavy wooden Greek infantry shield, faced with bronze, first introduced in the late eighth or early seventh century BC.

dory-spear.name: Doru
dory-spear.summary: The main spear of ancient Greek hoplites, about 2 to 3 metres long, built for phalanx combat rather than throwing.

epaminondas.name: Epaminondas
epaminondas.summary: Greek general and statesman (419/411–362 BC) who broke Spartan power at the Battle of Leuctra, freed the long-enslaved Messenian helots, and briefly made Thebes the leading power in Greek politics.

battle-of-leuctra.name: Battle of Leuctra
battle-of-leuctra.summary: 371 BC battle in which Theban forces decisively defeated Sparta, shattering Spartan dominance over Greece and beginning a short-lived Theban hegemony.

pelopidas.name: Pelopidas
pelopidas.summary: Theban statesman and general (died 364 BC) instrumental in establishing Thebes' brief mid-4th-century BC dominance over Greece.

sacred-band-of-thebes.name: Sacred Band of Thebes
sacred-band-of-thebes.summary: An elite unit of 300 Theban soldiers formed in 378 BC that helped win the Battle of Leuctra before being wiped out by Philip II and Alexander at Chaeronea in 338 BC.

philip-ii-of-macedon.name: Philip II of Macedon
philip-ii-of-macedon.summary: King of Macedon from 359 to 336 BC who built up its military power, defeated Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea in 338 BC, and was the father of Alexander the Great.

battle-of-chaeronea-338-bc.name: Battle of Chaeronea
battle-of-chaeronea-338-bc.summary: A 338 BC battle in which Philip II's Macedonian army decisively defeated an alliance of Greek city-states led by Athens and Thebes, making Philip the de facto ruler of Greece.

league-of-corinth.name: League of Corinth
league-of-corinth.summary: A federation of Greek city-states formed by Philip II of Macedon in 338–337 BC to unite Greece against Persia, later used by his son Alexander the Great.

mount-athos.name: Mount Athos
mount-athos.summary: Mountain and self-governing monastic region in Greece, a major center of Eastern Orthodox monastic life since at least the 9th century.

dardanelles.name: Dardanelles
dardanelles.summary: A narrow strait in northwestern Turkey, known in antiquity as the Hellespont, connecting the Sea of Marmara with the Aegean and separating Europe from Asia.

illyrian-wars.name: Illyrian Wars
illyrian-wars.summary: A series of wars between the Roman Republic and the Illyrian kingdom, starting in 229 BC when Rome crossed the Adriatic to stop piracy and expel Illyrian garrisons from Greek coastal towns.

teuta.name: Teuta
teuta.summary: Queen regent of the Ardiaei tribe in Illyria from about 231 to 228/227 BC, who lost the First Illyrian War to Rome and had to cede territory and pay tribute.

hoplitodromos.name: Hoplitodromos
hoplitodromos.summary: An ancient Greek footrace at the Olympic and other Panhellenic Games, first held in 520 BC, run in a hoplite's full armor including helmet and shield.

hesiod.name: Hesiod
hesiod.summary: Ancient Greek poet active around 750–650 BC, a near-contemporary of Homer, whose surviving works Theogony and Works and Days are major sources on Greek mythology, farming and early cosmology.

homeric-hymns.name: Homeric Hymns
homeric-hymns.summary: A collection of thirty-three ancient Greek hymns praising the gods, traditionally attributed to Homer though mostly dating to the 7th and 6th centuries BCE.

theogony.name: Theogony
theogony.summary: A poem by Hesiod, composed around 730–700 BC, describing the origins and genealogies of the Greek gods; one of the most important sources for early Greek cosmology.

works-and-days.name: Works and Days
works-and-days.summary: A didactic poem by the Greek poet Hesiod, written around 700 BC, mixing a farmer's almanac with moral advice and myths such as Prometheus and Pandora.

aeschylus.name: Aeschylus
aeschylus.summary: Ancient Greek tragedian (c. 525–456 BC), often called the father of tragedy, credited with expanding theatrical dialogue between characters.

sophocles.name: Sophocles
sophocles.summary: An ancient Greek tragedian (c. 497–406 BC) who wrote over 120 plays, of which seven survive, including Oedipus Rex and Antigone; he won 24 of 30 drama competitions.

euripides.name: Euripides
euripides.summary: A Greek tragedian of classical Athens (c. 480–406 BC), one of three tragedians whose plays survive, known for portraying mythical heroes as ordinary people in extraordinary circumstances.

oedipus-rex.name: Oedipus Rex
oedipus-rex.summary: An Athenian tragedy by Sophocles, first performed around 429 BCE, about Oedipus's search for his father's killer; now regarded as one of the greatest Greek tragedies.

antigone-sophocles-play.name: Antigone
antigone-sophocles-play.summary: An Athenian tragedy written by Sophocles around 442–440 BC, part of the Theban plays, about Antigone's defiance of King Creon to bury her brother's body.

ionia.name: Ionia
ionia.summary: An ancient region on the central western coast of Anatolia settled by Greek Ionians, home to twelve cities of the Ionian League and central to conflicts between Persia and Greece.

aristophanes.name: Aristophanes
aristophanes.summary: Ancient Greek comic playwright of Athens (c. 446–386 BC), known as "The Father of Comedy," whose surviving plays satirized real figures and events of his day.

menander.name: Menander
menander.summary: An Athenian playwright (c. 342–290 BC) and leading figure of Greek New Comedy, who wrote 108 comedies, most now known only through later Latin adaptations.

old-comedy.name: Old Comedy
old-comedy.summary: The earliest period of ancient Greek comedy, largely defined today by the surviving plays of Aristophanes, known for daring political satire and bawdy humor.

ancient-greek-comedy.name: New Comedy
ancient-greek-comedy.summary: The last of three periods of Athenian comedy, known mainly from substantial papyrus fragments of the playwright Menander, following the earlier Old and Middle Comedy periods.

alcaeus.name: Alcaeus
alcaeus.summary: Ancient Greek lyric poet from Lesbos (c. 625–580 BC) credited with inventing the Alcaic stanza and counted among the canonical nine lyric poets.

alcman.name: Alcman
alcman.summary: Ancient Greek choral lyric poet from Sparta (7th century BC), the earliest of the canonical Nine Lyric Poets, known mainly through fragments.

anacreon.name: Anacreon
anacreon.summary: Ancient Greek lyric poet (c. 573–c. 495 BC) known for drinking songs and erotic poems, later included among the canonical Nine Lyric Poets.

bacchylides.name: Bacchylides
bacchylides.summary: An ancient Greek lyric poet (c. 518–451 BC) ranked among the canonical Nine Lyric Poets, praised for clear, elegant verse and often compared with his contemporary Pindar.

ibycus.name: Ibycus
ibycus.summary: A 6th-century BC Greek lyric poet from Rhegium, counted among the nine canonical lyric poets of ancient Greece, whose surviving verses are known only from quotations and papyrus fragments.

longus.name: Longus
longus.summary: The presumed author of the ancient Greek romance Daphnis and Chloe, thought to have lived on Lesbos in the 2nd century AD; almost nothing else is known of him.

daphnis-and-chloe.name: Daphnis and Chloe
daphnis-and-chloe.summary: A Greek pastoral novel written during the Roman Empire, the only known work of the second-century writer Longus, about two young lovers on the island of Lesbos.

lesbos.name: Lesbos
lesbos.summary: A Greek island in the northeastern Aegean Sea, the third largest in Greece, whose capital Mytilene was traditionally founded around the 11th century BC.

linear-b.name: Linear B
linear-b.summary: A syllabic script for Mycenaean Greek, the earliest known form of Greek, dating from around 1450 BC and deciphered in 1952 by Michael Ventris.

boustrophedon.name: Boustrophedon
boustrophedon.summary: A writing style in which alternate lines run in reverse, mirror-image directions, common on ancient Greek inscriptions and other early scripts.

sappho.name: Sappho
sappho.summary: Ancient Greek lyric poet from Lesbos (c. 630–570 BC), celebrated in antiquity as one of the greatest poets, though most of her work now survives only in fragments.

pausanias-geographer.name: Pausanias (geographer)
pausanias-geographer.summary: A 2nd-century Greek traveler and geographer, c. 110 to 180, whose Description of Greece is a key source linking classical literature to archaeological sites.

description-of-greece.name: Description of Greece
description-of-greece.summary: A ten-book travel guide by the 2nd-century geographer Pausanias describing the geography, religious sites and myths of mainland Greece; it is the only surviving source about him.

nafpaktos.name: Nafpaktos
nafpaktos.summary: A Greek town on the Gulf of Corinth, known in antiquity as Naupactus, an important Athenian naval station in the Peloponnesian War, later called Lepanto under Venetian rule.

antonius-diogenes.name: Antonius Diogenes
antonius-diogenes.summary: Author, likely of the 2nd century AD, of the ancient Greek romance The Wonders Beyond Thule, a 24-book novel now lost except for a lengthy summary by Photios I of Constantinople.

photios-i-of-constantinople.name: Photios I of Constantinople
photios-i-of-constantinople.summary: Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople from 858 to 867 and 877 to 886 (c. 815–893), regarded as the most important intellectual of his era and a central figure in the conversion of the Slavs to Christianity.

aristarchus-of-samos.name: Aristarchus of Samos
aristarchus-of-samos.summary: Ancient Greek astronomer and mathematician (c. 310–230 BC) who proposed the first known heliocentric model, placing the Sun at the center of the universe.

philolaus.name: Philolaus
philolaus.summary: Greek Pythagorean philosopher (c. 470 – c. 385 BC) credited with the earliest known discussion of ideas leading to heliocentrism, including a 'Central Fire' at the center of the universe.

heraclides-ponticus.name: Heraclides Ponticus
heraclides-ponticus.summary: Greek philosopher and astronomer (c. 390–310 BC) best remembered for proposing that the Earth rotates on its axis, and sometimes credited as an early proponent of heliocentrism.

archytas.name: Archytas
archytas.summary: Ancient Greek mathematician, statesman and Pythagorean philosopher from Taras (435/410–360/350 BC), a friend of Plato reputed to have founded mathematical mechanics.

quadrivium.name: Quadrivium
quadrivium.summary: Medieval grouping of four mathematical arts—arithmetic, geometry, music and astronomy—taught alongside the trivium as part of the seven liberal arts.

hippocrates.name: Hippocrates
hippocrates.summary: A Greek physician and philosopher (c. 460–370 BC) traditionally called the 'Father of Medicine' for pioneering prognosis and clinical observation, and credited with the Hippocratic Oath.

galen.name: Galen
galen.summary: A Roman-era Greek physician, surgeon, and philosopher (129–c.216 CE) whose anatomical writings, shaped by the four-humors theory, dominated Western medicine for over 1,300 years.

humorism.name: Four Humors
humorism.summary: An ancient system of medicine, used by Greek and Roman physicians, holding that the body's workings depended on a balance of the four humors; it fell out of favor in the 17th century.

apollonius-of-perga.name: Apollonius of Perga
apollonius-of-perga.summary: An ancient Greek geometer and astronomer (c. 240-190 BC) who named the ellipse, parabola and hyperbola and is ranked among antiquity's greatest mathematicians.

eudoxus-of-cnidus.name: Eudoxus of Cnidus
eudoxus-of-cnidus.summary: An ancient Greek astronomer, mathematician, doctor and lawmaker (c. 390–340 BC) who studied under Archytas and Plato; none of his original works survive complete.

hipparchus.name: Hipparchus
hipparchus.summary: A Greek astronomer, geographer and mathematician (c. 190–120 BC) considered the founder of trigonometry, famous for discovering the precession of the equinoxes and often called the father of astronomy.

ptolemy.name: Ptolemy
ptolemy.summary: A Greco-Roman scholar of the 2nd century AD who wrote influential works on astronomy, geography and astrology; his geocentric model of the universe, promoted by the Catholic Church, was studied for over a thousand years.

antikythera-mechanism.name: Antikythera mechanism
antikythera-mechanism.summary: An ancient Greek analogue-computer device built in the 2nd century BC to predict astronomical positions and eclipses, discovered in a shipwreck in 1901.

conic-section.name: Conic sections
conic-section.summary: Curves—the hyperbola, parabola, and ellipse—formed where a plane cuts through a cone's surface, studied extensively by ancient Greek mathematicians such as Apollonius.

anaxagoras.name: Anaxagoras
anaxagoras.summary: Pre-Socratic Greek philosopher (c. 500–c. 428 BC) who introduced the concept of Nous as an ordering force and gave early scientific explanations of eclipses, the sun and rainbows.

aetolian-league.name: Aetolian League
aetolian-league.summary: An ancient Greek confederation of tribal communities and cities in central Greece, based at Thermon, that became a major Hellenistic power after defeating the Gauls in 279 BC before clashing with Macedon and later Rome.

byzantium.name: Byzantium
byzantium.summary: An ancient Greek city founded by colonists from Megara in the 7th century BC, later renamed Constantinople and, in modern times, Istanbul.

constantine-the-great.name: Constantine the Great
constantine-the-great.summary: Roman emperor from 306 to 337, the first to convert to Christianity, who legalized Christian worship across the empire and founded Constantinople as its new capital.

theodosius-i.name: Theodosius I
theodosius-i.summary: Roman emperor from 379 to 395, also called Theodosius the Great, who established Nicene Christianity as orthodox doctrine and was the last emperor to rule the whole Roman Empire.

sarissa.name: Sarissa
sarissa.summary: A long pike, 5 to 7 meters, introduced by Philip II of Macedon to strengthen the Macedonian phalanx, and used by Hellenistic armies for centuries after Alexander the Great's conquests.

herodotus.name: Herodotus
herodotus.summary: Greek historian and geographer (c. 484–c. 425 BC), called 'the Father of History' for his Histories, a detailed account of the Greco-Persian Wars and the peoples and lands around them.

alexander-i-of-macedon.name: Alexander I of Macedon
alexander-i-of-macedon.summary: King of ancient Macedonia from about 498 to 454 BC, nicknamed 'the Philhellene' for his support of Greece; his eldest son Perdiccas II succeeded him.

hellanodikai.name: Hellanodikai
hellanodikai.summary: The judges of the Ancient Olympic Games, responsible for upholding the rules and maintaining the games' standards.

argead-dynasty.name: Argead dynasty
argead-dynasty.summary: The ancient Macedonian royal house, also called the Temenid dynasty, that ruled Macedon from about 700 to 310 BC and included Philip II and Alexander the Great.

artaxerxes-ii.name: Artaxerxes II
artaxerxes-ii.summary: King of Kings of the Achaemenid Empire from 405/4 to 359/8 BC, who defeated his brother Cyrus the Younger's revolt and later faced further rebellions.

corinthian-war.name: Corinthian War
corinthian-war.summary: A conflict from 395 to 387 BC in which Sparta fought a coalition of Thebes, Athens, Corinth, and Argos, backed for a time by the Achaemenid Persian Empire.

peace-of-antalcidas.name: Peace of Antalcidas
peace-of-antalcidas.summary: A 387 BCE treaty, also called the King's Peace, guaranteed by the Persian king Artaxerxes II, that ended the Corinthian War and restored Persian control over Greek Ionia.

aeolis.name: Aeolis
aeolis.summary: A region on the coast of northwestern Asia Minor, home to Aeolian Greek city-states and islands including Lesbos.

perseus-of-macedon.name: Perseus of Macedon
perseus-of-macedon.summary: King of Macedon from 179 to 168 BC and last ruler of the Antigonid dynasty; his defeat by Rome at the Battle of Pydna ended Macedonia's independence.

third-macedonian-war.name: Third Macedonian War
third-macedonian-war.summary: A 171–168 BCE war between Rome and King Perseus of Macedon, ending in Rome's victory at Pydna, the fall of the Antigonid dynasty, and the end of Macedon's independence.

amphipolis.name: Amphipolis
amphipolis.summary: An ancient Greek city and former Athenian colony where Alexander the Great prepared for his invasion of Asia, and where his wife Roxana and son were later murdered.

pella.name: Pella
pella.summary: Capital of the ancient Greek kingdom of Macedon from the 4th century BC, birthplace of Philip II and Alexander the Great, sacked by Rome in 168 BC.

pelagonia.name: Pelagonia
pelagonia.summary: A geographical plain region of Macedonia, now shared between North Macedonia and Greece.

antigonus-ii-gonatas.name: Antigonus II Gonatas
antigonus-ii-gonatas.summary: Macedonian Greek ruler (c. 320–239 BC) who secured the Antigonid dynasty's hold on Macedon and won fame for defeating invading Gauls.

polybius.name: Polybius
polybius.summary: A Greek historian, about 200 to 118 BC, whose Histories chronicled Rome's rise to dominance from 264 to 146 BC; his ideas on checks and balances later influenced the framers of the US Constitution.

cleon-of-sicyon.name: Cleon of Sicyon
cleon-of-sicyon.summary: Tyrant who ruled the Greek city-state of Sicyon from about 300 to 280 BCE, later assassinated according to Plutarch.

aristotimus.name: Aristotimus
aristotimus.summary: Tyrant of the Greek city of Elis, installed by Macedonian king Antigonus II Gonatas in 272 BC, who ruled violently for only a few months before being killed by conspirators.

brennus-3rd-century-bc.name: Brennus
brennus-3rd-century-bc.summary: Gaulish leader who invaded the Greek mainland in 280–279 BCE, reaching Delphi to raid its treasury before being defeated and dying by suicide there in 279 BC.

ptolemy-ceraunus.name: Ptolemy Ceraunus
ptolemy-ceraunus.summary: A son of Ptolemy I Soter who was passed over for the Egyptian throne, then seized the throne of Macedon around 281 BC and ruled it for seventeen months before dying in battle against invading Gauls in 279 BC.

mark-antony.name: Mark Antony
mark-antony.summary: Roman politician and general (83–30 BC) and ally of Julius Caesar who, after Caesar's assassination, formed the Second Triumvirate with Octavian and Lepidus and later allied with Cleopatra.

second-triumvirate.name: Second Triumvirate
second-triumvirate.summary: A commission formed in 43 BC giving Mark Antony, Lepidus and Octavian near-absolute power over Rome, formally lasting until 32 BC and ending with civil war and the defeat of Caesar's assassins.

battle-of-philippi.name: Battle of Philippi
battle-of-philippi.summary: The final 42 BC battle of the Liberators' civil war, fought in two engagements at Philippi in Macedonia, in which Mark Antony and Octavian defeated Julius Caesar's assassins Brutus and Cassius, who both died by suicide.

augustus.name: Augustus
augustus.summary: Founder of the Roman Empire, ruling as its first emperor from 27 BC until his death in AD 14, and known earlier as Octavian.

achaia-roman-province.name: Achaea
achaia-roman-province.summary: Roman province covering the Peloponnese, Attica and other parts of Greece, annexed in 146 BC and made separate under Augustus; a prosperous, senatorial province and center of Greek learning.

archelaus-of-macedon.name: Archelaus of Macedon
archelaus-of-macedon.summary: King of Macedon from 413 to 399 BC, a capable ruler credited with strengthening the kingdom's military, administration and commerce more than any predecessor.

orestes-of-macedon.name: Orestes of Macedon
orestes-of-macedon.summary: King of ancient Macedon who reigned from 400/399 to 398/7 BC before being deposed or killed by his uncle and guardian, Aeropus II.

aeropus-ii-of-macedon.name: Aeropus II of Macedon
aeropus-ii-of-macedon.summary: King of ancient Macedonia from 398/7 BC until his death around 394/3 BC, who ruled after allegedly murdering his young nephew Orestes.

amyntas-ii-of-macedon.name: Amyntas II of Macedon
amyntas-ii-of-macedon.summary: King of ancient Macedon for a few months around 394/3 BC, who took the throne after Aeropus II's death and was soon afterward assassinated.

pausanias-of-macedon.name: Pausanias of Macedon
pausanias-of-macedon.summary: King of ancient Macedon for about a year, 394/3 to 393/2 BCE, following the brief preceding reign of Amyntas II after his father Aeropus II's death; he was later assassinated and succeeded by Amyntas III.

andriscus.name: Andriscus
andriscus.summary: A Greek pretender who became the last independent king of Macedon in 149 BC, claiming descent from the last legitimate Macedonian king; his one-year reign ended when Rome defeated him.

fourth-macedonian-war.name: Fourth Macedonian War
fourth-macedonian-war.summary: A 150-148 BC war in which Rome crushed the pretender Andriscus's revived Macedonian kingdom, after which Rome made Macedon a province.

quintus-caecilius-metellus-macedonicus.name: Quintus Caecilius Metellus Macedonicus
quintus-caecilius-metellus-macedonicus.summary: A Roman Republic statesman and general (c. 188–116/115 BC) who served as praetor, consul, proconsul and censor, gaining his title after defeating the Macedonians in the Fourth Macedonian War.

battle-of-pydna-148-bc.name: Battle of Pydna (148 BC)
battle-of-pydna-148-bc.summary: A 148 BC battle in which Rome's Quintus Caecilius Metellus defeated the Macedonian pretender Andriscus, ending the Fourth Macedonian War and Macedon's last independent political force, which became a Roman province.

thales-of-miletus.name: Thales of Miletus
thales-of-miletus.summary: A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher from Miletus, c. 626-548 BC, often called the first philosopher for explaining nature without myth; he held that everything derives from water.

pre-socratic-philosophy.name: Pre-Socratic philosophy
pre-socratic-philosophy.summary: Ancient Greek philosophy before Socrates, beginning in the 6th century BC, which sought to explain the origin and nature of the universe through natural law rather than the gods.

socrates.name: Socrates
socrates.summary: Ancient Greek philosopher from Athens (c. 470–399 BC), often called the first Western moral philosopher, known through his students Plato and Xenophon; sentenced to death for impiety.

aristotle.name: Aristotle
aristotle.summary: Ancient Greek philosopher and polymath (384–322 BC) who founded the Peripatetic school, tutored Alexander the Great, and laid groundwork for modern science.

battle-of-actium.name: Battle of Actium
battle-of-actium.summary: A naval battle fought on 2 September 31 BCE in which Octavian's fleet, aided by Marcus Agrippa, defeated the combined forces of Mark Antony and Cleopatra, the climax of their long rivalry.

stoicism.name: Stoicism
stoicism.summary: A philosophical movement from Hellenistic Greece into the Roman Imperial period, teaching self-discipline and virtue as the path to a calm, rational, well-reasoned life.

epicureanism.name: Epicureanism
epicureanism.summary: A school of philosophy founded in 307 BCE on the teachings of Epicurus, holding that modest pleasure and freedom from pain and fear, reached through knowledge and limited desires, is life's highest good.

a-c-grayling.name: A. C. Grayling
a-c-grayling.summary: British philosopher and author, born 1949, who has written around 30 books on philosophy, ethics and the history of ideas and founded New College of the Humanities in 2011.

epicurus.name: Epicurus
epicurus.summary: Greek philosopher (341–270 BC) who founded Epicureanism, teaching that managing desires, removing fears, and friendship lead to a pleasant, happy life; he taught at his school 'The Garden' in Athens.

pyrrho.name: Pyrrho
pyrrho.summary: Greek philosopher (c. 360–270 BC) from Elis, considered the first Greek skeptic and founder of the school of thought later called Pyrrhonism.

timon-of-phlius.name: Timon of Phlius
timon-of-phlius.summary: Ancient Greek philosopher (c. 320–235 BC) and student of Pyrrho whose satirical poetry helped shape the skeptic tradition.

platonic-academy.name: Platonic Academy
platonic-academy.summary: A school founded by Plato around 387 BC in Athens where Aristotle later studied for twenty years; regarded as the first institution of higher education in the West.

arcesilaus.name: Arcesilaus
arcesilaus.summary: Greek Hellenistic philosopher (c. 316–241 BC) who founded Academic Skepticism as head of the Platonic Academy, doubting that the senses could reveal certain truth.

peripatetic-school.name: Peripatetic school
peripatetic-school.summary: A philosophical school founded by Aristotle in Athens in 335 BC, continuing his teachings on virtue and moderation after his death and reviving under Rome.

theophrastus.name: Theophrastus
theophrastus.summary: An ancient Greek philosopher (c. 371–287 BC) who succeeded Aristotle as head of the Lyceum and is considered the father of botany for his works on plants.

strato-of-lampsacus.name: Strato of Lampsacus
strato-of-lampsacus.summary: Peripatetic philosopher (c. 335 to c. 269 BCE) who led the Lyceum after Theophrastus and emphasized natural science over the need for an active god.

eudaimonia.name: Eudaimonia
eudaimonia.summary: A Greek word for happiness or welfare, treated by Aristotle as the highest human good and a central concept in ancient ethics alongside virtue and practical wisdom.

speusippus.name: Speusippus
speusippus.summary: An ancient Greek philosopher (about 408 to 339/8 BC) and Plato's nephew, who led Plato's Academy after his death but rejected the Theory of Forms.

xenocrates.name: Xenocrates
xenocrates.summary: Greek philosopher and mathematician (c. 396/5-314/3 BC) who led Plato's Academy from 339/8 BC, refining Plato's ideas with mathematical elements and teaching that virtue produces happiness.

theory-of-forms.name: Theory of Forms
theory-of-forms.summary: A philosophical theory credited to Plato holding that non-physical, unchangeable Forms are more real than the physical objects that merely resemble them.

academic-skepticism.name: Academic skepticism
academic-skepticism.summary: A philosophy from Plato's Academy (c. 266–90 BC) holding that certain knowledge is impossible, though degrees of plausibility allow action; known mainly through Cicero's Academica.

cicero.name: Cicero
cicero.summary: A Roman statesman, lawyer, philosopher and orator (106–43 BC) who served as consul in 63 BC and greatly shaped the Latin language through his surviving writings.

academica-cicero.name: Academica
academica-cicero.summary: A partly lost philosophical work by Cicero, published in two editions from 45 BCE, aimed at popularizing Academic Skepticism in Rome.

sulla.name: Sulla
sulla.summary: Roman general and statesman (138–78 BC) who became the first to march on Rome and win a civil war, then ruled as dictator and enacted constitutional reforms.

aenesidemus.name: Aenesidemus
aenesidemus.summary: 1st-century BC Greek philosopher from Knossos who revived Pyrrhonist skepticism and introduced ten skeptical "modes" for suspending judgment.

pyrrhonism.name: Pyrrhonism
pyrrhonism.summary: An Ancient Greek school of philosophical skepticism founded by Aenesidemus in the 1st century BCE, inspired by Pyrrho and Timon of Phlius, urging suspension of judgment on all beliefs.

zarmanochegas.name: Zarmanochegas
zarmanochegas.summary: An Indian gymnosophist, or 'naked philosopher', possibly of the Sramana tradition, who reportedly burned himself to death in Athens around 19 BC after meeting Nicholas of Damascus.

nicolaus-of-damascus.name: Nicolaus of Damascus
nicolaus-of-damascus.summary: Greek historian, diplomat and philosopher (c. 64 BC–after 4 AD) who wrote a vast universal history, now mostly lost, plus lives of Augustus and Herod.

antioch.name: Antioch
antioch.summary: An ancient city in northern Syria founded in 300 BC that became capital of the Seleucid Empire and later a major center of Roman Syria and early Christianity.

plutarch.name: Plutarch
plutarch.summary: A Greek and Roman philosopher, historian and biographer (before 50–after 120 AD) best known for Parallel Lives, biographies of famous Greeks and Romans.

dionysia.name: Dionysia
dionysia.summary: A major ancient Athenian festival honoring the god Dionysus, featuring processions, sacrifices, and theatrical performances of tragedies and comedies.

dionysus.name: Dionysus
dionysus.summary: Greek god of wine-making, festivity, ecstatic ritual and theatre, whose followers believed they became possessed by him; his origins are uncertain, possibly Mycenaean.

hera.name: Hera
hera.summary: Ancient Greek goddess of marriage, women and family, queen of the Olympian gods as sister and wife of Zeus, known for her jealous response to his affairs.

olympia-greece.name: Olympia, Greece
olympia-greece.summary: Ancient sanctuary in the Peloponnese dedicated mainly to Zeus, where the ancient Olympic Games were held every four years from the 8th century BC.

panhellenic-games.name: Panhellenic Games
panhellenic-games.summary: Collective term for four ancient Greek religious festivals with athletic contests -- the Olympic, Pythian, Nemean and Isthmian Games -- each honoring a different god.

lykaia.name: Lykaia
lykaia.summary: A secretive ancient Greek festival on Mount Lykaion in Arcadia, held yearly around early May, whose myths and rites centred on cannibalism and a possible werewolf transformation for young male participants.

arcadia-region.name: Arcadia
arcadia-region.summary: A region in the central Peloponnese, Greece, named for the mythological Arcas and considered in myth the home of Hermes and Pan; later idealized in European Renaissance art.

pan-god.name: Pan
pan-god.summary: Ancient Greek god of the wild, shepherds, flocks and rustic music, shown with the legs and horns of a goat and linked to fertility and spring.

delos.name: Delos
delos.summary: A tiny Greek island near Mykonos revered as the mythical birthplace of Apollo and Artemis, sacred for a millennium and now a major archaeological site.

serapis.name: Serapis
serapis.summary: A Graeco-Egyptian god formed by blending Osiris and Apis, promoted from the 3rd century BC by Ptolemy I Soter to unite his Greek and Egyptian subjects, and later popular across the Roman Empire.

isis.name: Isis
isis.summary: A major ancient Egyptian goddess, first recorded in the Old Kingdom, who resurrected her husband Osiris and protected their son Horus; her worship later spread across the Greco-Roman world.

atargatis.name: Atargatis
atargatis.summary: Chief goddess of northern Syria in classical antiquity, primarily a fertility deity also responsible for protecting her city and people, with her chief sanctuary at Hierapolis.

hadad.name: Hadad
hadad.summary: Storm- and rain-god of Canaanite and ancient Mesopotamian religion, also called Adad or Baʿal, symbolized by the bull and later equated with Zeus and Jupiter.
